Stated Claim / Post Context:
Father left his daughter $100 after he said she 'disowned' him - then a judge found flaws in his 'DIY will' that gave her a share of his estate

Neville thought his will would have the final say: a home for three sons, and just $100 for the daughter who 'disowned' him. But flaws in his 'DIY' will have caused a bitter legal fight.

Actual Article Body:
By SARAH BROOKES - SENIOR REPORTER, AUSTRALIA

Published:  00:23 AEDT, 30 October 2026   |  Updated:  00:23 AEDT, 30 October 2026

A Queensland father's attempt to cut his eldest daughter out of his will with a token $100 inheritance has backfired after a Supreme Court judge ruled key parts of his rambling handwritten will were legally ineffective, meaning she will now share in part of the estate after all.

Neville Cecil Huxley, who died in 2021 aged 80, left a DIY 'kit will' dividing much of his estate between nine of his 11 children still living while expressly excluding daughter Tina Gilbert, whom he said had 'disowned' him in 1989.

But a bitter family dispute over the will has dragged on for years, prompting a judge to warn that the 'vast majority' of the modest $428,000 estate could be consumed by legal fees before the beneficiaries receive their inheritance.

In the handwritten 2013 will, Mr Huxley directed that money remaining in his bank accounts be shared between nine of his children, adding: 'It is my intention to specifically exclude my daughter Tina Gilbert from the aforementioned gift because I have made a specific gift for her in this will with an explanation as to why.'

Elsewhere in the document, he wrote that 'my daughter tina gilbert (sic) is to be given $100 because she had disowned me in 1989 for unknown reasons or explanation - my only gift to her'.

The will also attempted to preserve a family property near Charters Towers for three of Neville's sons, who live with Fragile X syndrome, a genetic condition that can cause intellectual disability and require support with everyday tasks.

'My property is to stay in the family for my sons to live in the family home,' the will stated.

The court heard the brothers require varying levels of support in their daily lives and live in supported accommodation rather than at the property itself.

Neville Huxley (pictured) was described in a funeral notice as a self-made jack-of-all-trades

Eight of the 11 children of the late Neville Huxley are pictured in the back row (left to right: Ronnel, Aaron, Nicole, Neville Jnr, Jennifer, Catherine, Sandra and Clifford)

Justice Johnstone warned that unless the long-running dispute is resolved soon, the 'vast majority' of the $428,000 estate, including this modest Millchester property, could be consumed by legal fees

However, Justice Johnstone found several directions in the homemade will were invalid and that the clause dealing with the property failed to create any legally enforceable life interest for the sons.

As a result, that part of the estate must be distributed under Queensland intestacy laws.

The outcome means that Tina, despite her father's stated wish that she receive only $100, will share in part of the estate under the intestacy rules.

Justice Johnstone noted the estate was worth about $428,000 but warned that unless the administration could be finalised soon, 'the vast majority of the estate will be lost to legal fees'.

'There have already been a number of court hearings in the matter. The costs will already be significant... unless the administration of the estate can be finalised soon, the vast majority of the estate will be lost to legal fees,' he wrote.

The judge said the administration of the estate had been plagued by 'profound delay' since probate was granted in 2021.

The court heard daughter and co-executor Ellen had been attempting to progress the administration of the estate through her solicitor, while her sister and fellow executor, Catherine, had not.

Catherine acknowledged there had been delays but blamed her former solicitors; however, Justice Johnstone said she had offered no direct evidence to support that claim.

Neville and Shirley Huxley (pictured) married in 1969 and had 11 children. Shirley passed away in 2008 from cancer

Supreme Court Justice Christopher Johnstone said the administration of the estate had been plagued by 'profound delay' since probate was granted in 2021

In an extraordinary aside, the judge revealed a solicitor acting for Catherine told a previous directions hearing that a fixed-fee retainer had been exhausted and that he was 'sick of it' – referring to the long-running family dispute.

The judgment also records that a court form was filed incorrectly stating the judge had granted leave for the law firm to withdraw from the matter.

'What was stated in that form was false,' Justice Johnstone wrote.

Despite years of litigation, the judge left Catherine in place as an executor for now, expressing hope his ruling on the disputed will would finally allow the estate to be wound up and distributed.

'Whilst it may be the case that the first respondent has not received much in the way of helpful assistance from her most recent representation, that does not explain her conduct over the preceding five years since the grant of probate was made,' he said.

The family feud boiled over when daughter Ellen offered to buy the estate's land and collection of vehicles and machinery at market value, a proposal opposed by her sisters.

Initially, Jennifer played only a limited role in the proceedings, seeking the appointment of a litigation guardian for three beneficiaries.

But she later 'entered the fray' alongside Catherine, with the judge noting their interests had become aligned in opposition to Ellen's application.

The disputed property is occupied rent-free by Jennifer, who the court said appeared to perform general caretaking duties and who was appointed as guardian for two of her brothers together with Catherine.

Neville Huxley (pictured front centre) with seven of his children

She told the court her brothers Clifford, Neville and Arron regularly visited the property and that Arron – whose name was also sometimes spelled 'Aaron' – often stayed overnight during periods of her care.

Neville, who was born in Mount Isa in 1941, was described in a funeral notice as a self-made jack-of-all-trades who worked on prawn trawlers and cattle stations despite being unable to properly read or write.

He later settled near Charters Towers, unsuccessfully ran for mayor in the 1980s and spent much of his later life tinkering with cars and caring for horses.

The estate includes land valued at about $160,000 and a collection of old car bodies, parts and machinery valued at $86,450. The deceased also held more than $180,000 in cash across two bank accounts.

The irony of the case is that despite Mr Huxley's express wish that his estranged daughter receive only $100, she will now share in part of the estate because of the way his homemade will was drafted.
